strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated bottleneck: edge-centric memory materialization in equivariant GNNs, and clearly frames the question of whether equivariant attention can support FlashAttention-style streaming execution.

The algebraic core (EAAS, Proposition 4.3) is supported by a complete derivation in Appendix B, including the real-vs-complex CG basis change, parity selection rules, and concrete low-degree worked examples, which strengthens confidence in exactness of the SO(3)→SO(2) sparsification.

The fused Triton kernel with online softmax (Algorithm 1) is a concrete, well-specified implementation of the node-centric streaming formulation, and the paper is honest that the scalar attention weight is the only edge-dependent term.

Experiments span accuracy (SPICE subsets, OMol25), kernel-level throughput/memory (Figure 4), end-to-end inference scaling to 100k atoms (Table 3), and a physically meaningful MD validation (water RDF), giving multiple angles of evidence.
Code is released, and appendices give nontrivial benchmarking detail (timing protocol, OOM handling, input generation, kernel configuration overrides), which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Headline speedup claims are measured against weak baselines. The 'FlashAttention' baseline in Figure 1/Appendix A is dense SDPA with a mask (attention over all N atoms), and the 20× TFLOPS comparison is against a 'naive PyTorch implementation'. A fair, strong baseline (e.g., a dedicated sparse flash-attention kernel such as torch-sphinx/flash-attn with varlen over neighbor blocks) is missing, so the 20× and the Figure 1 gaps are likely inflated.

The 'O(|V|) activation memory' claim is not fully substantiated: the neighbor index tensor I ∈ Z^{N×K}, the edge-dependent bias b(r_ij), radial terms ϕ(r_ij), and the per-node rotations D_R are all O(NK) or per-edge quantities whose handling in the backward pass (recomputation cost) is not analyzed. 'Linear activation memory' should be stated more carefully.

Internal inconsistencies: the text claims the conservative variant achieves aggregate Energy MAE of 1.27 meV/atom on OMol25 'matching eSEN-small', but Table 2 reports E2V2-Cons total E = 2.09 (and Direct = 1.24); similarly the SPICE narrative overstates 'lowest Energy and Force MAE across most subsets' while eSEN-Cons clearly wins on the ALL column (0.23/6.36 vs 0.57/7.80).

No ablation isolating the accuracy impact of EAAS vs. the attention reformulation vs. the kernel; no wall-clock training-time vs. accuracy trade-off against E2Former-V1 or eSEN at matched compute, which is the claim that matters most ('maintains comparable predictive performance while accelerating').

Parity handling is deferred ('we omit the parity for notational simplicity'), yet parity is essential for molecular potentials; how the re-indexing operator P extends to O(3) irreps is not specified. There is also a citation error: eSEN is attributed to Passaro & Zitnick (2023), which is eSCN (eSEN is Fu et al., 2025).

Reproducibility gaps: training configuration (GPUs, steps, hyperparameters, L_max, channel counts) for the SPICE/OMol25 results is not provided, and the abstract's code link is truncated ('The code is avalible at'), suggesting a rushed manuscript with several typos ('tow datasets', 'avalible').

OOM entries in Table 3 may partly reflect baseline default configurations rather than fundamental limits; no attempt was made to make baselines memory-efficient, which weakens the scalability comparison.

strengths: The paper targets a real and timely bottleneck: edge-centric tensor materialization in SO(3)-equivariant GNNs, and the node-centric reformulation with a fused Triton kernel (Algorithm 1) is a sensible, well-motivated engineering contribution that brings FlashAttention-style streaming to equivariant attention.

The algebraic development (Appendix B) is careful: the parity-dependent re-indexing rule is derived from Clebsch–Gordan selection rules in both complex and real bases, with concrete low-degree examples, and the derivation claims exact equivariance rather than an approximation.

The evaluation spans microbenchmarks (Figure 3, Figure 4), accuracy on SPICE (Table 1), scalability on OMol25 (Table 2), inference throughput up to 100k atoms (Table 3), and a physical sanity check via water RDF (Figure 5). Appendix A and D give reasonable benchmarking detail (warmup/timing protocol, OOM handling, system generation).
The demonstration that a transformer-based equivariant model can run at 100k atoms where prior equivariant transformers OOM is a practically useful result for the atomistic ML community.
weaknesses: Overstated headline claims relative to the evidence. The '20× TFLOPS improvement' and Figure 1 comparisons are against a naive PyTorch edge-centric implementation, and the 'FlashAttention' baseline is a sparse masked SDPA with a pre-built mask — not a strong, purpose-built sparse graph attention baseline. The abstract's framing ('20× improvement... compared to standard implementations') conflates naive and standard.

Accuracy claims are not consistently supported by the tables. The text claims 'lowest Energy and Force MAE across most subsets' and the conclusion claims 'superior performance on molecular benchmarks', yet on the SPICE aggregate eSEN-Cons (0.23/6.36) clearly beats both E2V2 variants (0.53/8.27). On OMol25, the text states the conservative variant achieves 1.27 meV/atom total, but Table 2 reports E2V2-Cons. at 2.09 — a text/table inconsistency that undermines confidence in the reported results.

Limited originality: EAAS is essentially eSCN's SO(3)→SO(2) axis-aligned sparsification applied to the E2Former Wigner-6j factorization, and the kernel applies standard FlashAttention tiling/online-softmax to this setting. The contribution is a combination of known techniques rather than a new method or new understanding, which should be stated more modestly.

Reproducibility is compromised: the abstract states 'The code is avalible at' with an incomplete URL (and a typo), so the claimed code release cannot be verified. Typos ('tow datasets') and the text/table mismatch above suggest insufficient polish.

Missing experimental details weaken the accuracy comparisons: model size, training budget, and hyperparameters for E2V2 on SPICE/OMol25 are not reported, so it is unclear whether comparisons against MACE, eSEN, and UMA are compute- or parameter-matched.

Contribution 3 claims improved training throughput and memory efficiency, but the experiments primarily measure inference; no training-throughput results are presented. Training-time cost of the alignment/re-indexing pipeline (rotation matrices per edge/node) is not analyzed.

The MD validation is thin: a single oxygen–oxygen RDF on one 216-molecule water system, with no quantitative error metric, trajectory length, or stability statistics, is not sufficient to support the claim of 'high-fidelity reproduction of complex many-body interactions'.

Several design details are under-specified: the learnable radial scaling φ(r_ij) and bias b(r_ij) are not characterized; the 'parity component' / ablation of EAAS vs. the plain 6j factorization on end-task accuracy is absent, so it is hard to tell how much accuracy (if any) the algebraic changes cost or gain.

strengths: The core idea is compelling and well-motivated: combining the node-centric Wigner-6j factorization of E2Former (Li et al., 2025) with an eSCN-style SO(3)→SO(2) axis-aligned sparsification (EAAS) and a FlashAttention-style fused Triton kernel addresses a genuine, widely recognized memory/latency bottleneck in equivariant architectures, and the paper convincingly identifies the gap between theoretical O(|V|) complexity and practical hardware realization.

The algebraic development is unusually careful for a systems-oriented paper: Lemma 4.1, Definition 4.2, and Proposition 4.3 are supported by a complete derivation in Appendix B (complex-to-real basis change, selection rules, parity-dependent collapse, and concrete low-degree worked examples), which supports the claim of exact equivariance preservation.

The evaluation is broad: kernel-level microbenchmarks (TFLOPS and peak memory vs. neighbors and atoms, Figure 4), accuracy on SPICE (Table 1) and OMol25 (Table 2), inference throughput scaling to 100k atoms against many strong baselines (Table 3), and an MD simulation sanity check (RDF, Figure 5). The demonstrated ability to run at 100k atoms where EquiformerV2, E2Former-V1, and MACE-Large OOM is a practically significant result.

The appendices provide substantial reproducibility detail (timing protocols, baseline implementation sketches, FCC supercell generation, configuration overrides), and the online-softmax streaming algorithm is clearly specified (Algorithm 1).
weaknesses: The headline speedups are measured against weak or ambiguous baselines. The 20× TFLOPS and 16–19× memory comparisons (Figure 4) are against a 'naive PyTorch implementation' of the authors' own formulation, not against well-optimized existing implementations (e.g., eSCN's optimized SO(2) convolutions, MACE's CUDA kernels). In Figure 1, the 'FlashAttention' baseline uses dense N×N SDPA with a pre-built mask — not how sparse attention would be implemented in practice — and 'Traditional EGNNs' is the authors' own PyTorch edge-centric reimplementation rather than a published model. The claimed advantages are therefore likely overstated relative to a properly optimized field baseline.

Accuracy claims are inconsistent with the reported results. The contributions list claims 'superior performance,' but on SPICE (Table 1) E2Former-V2 is worse than eSEN-Cons overall (0.23/6.36 vs. 0.53/8.27) and its force MAE is worse than E2Former-V1 on several subsets (e.g., ALL: 8.27 vs 7.46). 'Comparable performance' would be the defensible claim; 'superior' is not supported.

There is a text–table inconsistency on the OMol25 results: Section 5.3 states the conservative variant achieves an aggregate Energy MAE of 1.27 meV/atom 'matching eSEN-small,' but Table 2 reports E2V2-Cons total E of 2.09 (E2V2-Direct is 1.24). This materially affects the claimed competitiveness on the flagship large-scale benchmark and must be resolved.

The paper does not address translation equivariance. The factorization in Eq. (5) uses solid spherical harmonics of absolute positions R(r_i) and R(r_j); under a global translation these quantities change, and the manuscript never discusses how translational symmetry is preserved — a fundamental property for atomistic potentials. This theoretical gap needs an explicit explanation or proof.

The O(|V|) activation memory claim is narrower than presented: neighbor indices, radial encodings b(r_ij)/φ(r_ij), and the gather structure remain O(|E|); the claim holds only for attention intermediates, and the paper does not report end-to-end training-time memory or throughput, despite the contributions claiming training efficiency advantages.

There are no model-level ablations isolating the contribution of EAAS versus the fused attention kernel (Figure 3 is a kernel-only benchmark), no parameter counts, and no seeds/variance reporting for accuracy results.

Presentation and citation sloppiness undermines confidence: the abstract ends with 'The code is avalible at' with no URL (a reproducibility red flag), eSEN is misattributed to Passaro & Zitnick (2023) (that is eSCN; eSEN is Fu et al., 2025) in Sections 5.3–5.4, the naming oscillates between E2Former-V2 and E2FormerV2, and there are typos ('avalible', 'the tow datasets').
The MD evaluation (Figure 5) is a single qualitative RDF plot against MACE-OFF Medium with no quantitative metric or error analysis, yet the text claims 'superior structural alignment.'

strengths: Identifies a real and important bottleneck: edge-centric tensor materialization in SO(3)-equivariant GNNs, and delivers a coherent end-to-end solution combining algebraic sparsification (EAAS) with a fused, node-centric streaming attention kernel, achieving genuine O(N) activation memory.

The algebraic contribution is carefully derived and verified: Lemma 4.1 (pole sparsity), Proposition 4.3, and the full derivation of the re-indexing operator P from Clebsch-Gordan structure, including real-vs-complex basis conventions and concrete low-degree examples (Appendix C).

EAAS is benchmarked against strong, optimized third-party backends (cuEquivariance, OpenEquivariance), not just naive baselines, showing 1.5-3.6x speedups, which supports the claim that the gains are structural (Table 3).

Broad and varied empirical validation: SPICE and OMol25 accuracy (competitive or best on most subsets), OC20 S2EF-2M, throughput scaling from 1k to 100k atoms where baselines OOM, component ablation (Table 4), neighbor-density sensitivity (Appendix E), and physical validation via bulk-water RDF and a 2ns, 30k-atom protein MD trajectory.

Unusually honest treatment of tradeoffs for this area: Appendix D explicitly discusses the expressivity cost of moving non-linearity off the edge value path; Appendix J openly reports that dense FlashAttention achieves far higher absolute TFLOPS and that the kernel runs in FP32; Appendix E shows the edge-centric baseline can be faster for very sparse graphs (k<=2).

Reproducibility is good: training hyperparameters, backbone configuration, benchmark protocol (warmup/timed iterations, memory reset, OOM handling), reference implementation snippets for Figure 1 baselines, and a stated code release.
weaknesses: Headline claims are inflated relative to the evidence: the abstract's '20x higher TFLOPS' is measured against a naive PyTorch implementation, whereas Appendix J (Table 12) shows the fused sparse kernel reaches only ~0.6-2 TFLOPS versus 6.5-38.6 TFLOPS for dense SDPA on the same GPU. The kernel wins on memory scaling, not raw throughput, and the framing should reflect that.

Figure 1's 'FlashAttention' baseline is dense masked SDPA, which scales quadratically in N; the claim that 'the advantage of our method becomes increasingly pronounced as N grows' is largely a consequence of comparing a sparse method against a dense one, and the strongest baselines (optimized sparse attention kernels) are absent from the headline comparison.

There is some tension between the O(N) / fully node-centric claim and the actual formulation: attention scores and the edge feature Fea_ij in Appendix D are still edge-level quantities computed per edge (O(kN) work); the claim holds only for activation memory, and the paper is not always careful to distinguish memory from compute complexity in the abstract and introduction.

The attention mechanism restricts attention weights to SO(3)-invariant scalars (Eq. 7), a real expressivity reduction relative to EquiformerV2/eSEN-style equivariant attention; the empirical mitigation via the Appendix D construction is plausible but the accuracy margins over strong baselines like eSEN are modest, and the effect of this design choice is not isolated (e.g., no ablation of the QKdotS_alpha vs. richer attention variants).

Minor consistency issues: Definition 4.2 states m_i = m_o while the odd-parity branch re-indexes m_i -> -m_o (clarified only in Appendix C); the benchmark configuration uses max_neighbors=32 with a 6A cutoff while the throughput benchmark assumes ~50 neighbors per atom, creating ambiguity about which regime the headline numbers reflect; the training-throughput claim in the contributions is only partially substantiated (Table 4 is the main end-to-end evidence).

MD validation is limited to two qualitative demonstrations (water RDF, a single protein TM-score trajectory) without error statistics, diffusion coefficients, or comparisons beyond MACE-OFF, so the 'physically faithful MD' claim is only weakly supported.

strengths: The mathematical development is careful and complete: the EAAS re-indexing operator is derived exactly from Clebsch-Gordan structure (Lemma 4.1, Proposition 4.3, Appendix B/C with parity selection rules, sign conventions, and worked low-degree examples), so the 'exactness' claim is well-supported rather than asserted.

The system contribution is real and relevant: a fused, node-centric Triton kernel with online softmax (Algorithm 1) that eliminates O(|E|) edge materialization is a meaningful extension of FlashAttention-style execution to SO(3)-equivariant attention, where this was genuinely unexplored.

Evaluation breadth is above average for this area: accuracy on SPICE and OMol25, an additional OC20 S2EF-2M result (Table 8), microbenchmarks against strong optimized backends (cuEquivariance, OpenEquivariance — not just e3nn), an end-to-end component ablation (Table 4), neighbor-density sensitivity analysis (Appendix E), and physical validation via water RDF and a 30k-atom protein MD trajectory.

The paper is commendably honest in places: Appendix J openly reports that the fused kernel is substantially slower than dense FlashAttention in absolute TFLOPS and explains why, and Appendix E admits edge-centric baselines can win at very small k. The kernel-efficiency claims are also grounded in comparisons against genuinely optimized third-party kernels (Table 3), not only a strawman.
Attention design choices (invariant query/key, equivariant value path) and the non-linearity trade-off relative to EquiformerV2/eSEN are explicitly discussed (Appendix D) rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The headline 'up to 20x higher TFLOPS' is measured against a naive PyTorch edge-centric implementation, which is a weak baseline. Against a fair dense SDPA baseline (Table 12), the proposed kernel is ~6-60x slower in TFLOPS; the abstract and contributions do not qualify this, and Figure 1's 'FlashAttention' curve (a masked SDPA, known to degrade severely at large N) is presented in a way that flatters the method.

The abstract literally ends mid-sentence ('Our released code can be found at' with no URL), and I could not find a working code link elsewhere. For a paper whose central contribution is a systems/kernel artifact and which claims 'released code', this is a serious reproducibility gap at submission time.

Benchmark fairness is questionable in places: Table 10 reports training with max_neighbors=32 and a 6 A cutoff, while the throughput benchmark (Appendix H) uses ~50 neighbors per atom, potentially favoring the node-centric design relative to how baselines were configured. Also, parameter counts of compared models are not reported in Table 5 (only in the OC20 table), so throughput comparisons across heterogeneous model sizes are hard to interpret.

The claim of 'matching eSEN-small' on OMol25 is generous: E2V2-Cons is worse than eSEN on biomolecules and electrolytes (energy), and E2V2-Direct is worse on most domains (Table 2). Overall accuracy is 'competitive' rather than 'preserved' in the strict sense; the abstract's 'preserves predictive accuracy' slightly overstates.

The contribution of EAAS relative to the fused kernel is modest: Table 4 shows EAAS alone gives ~1.5x at 5k atoms and cannot prevent OOM at 10k atoms, while the kernel provides the dominant gain. The framing elevates EAAS to a co-equal headline contribution when the evidence suggests it is secondary.

The intro/related-work claim that these execution principles 'remain unexplored in existing SO(3)-equivariant architectures' overlooks adjacent systems work (e.g., the cuEquivariance/OpenEquivariance kernels and SO(2)-reduction line of eSCN/EquiformerV2), and the paper builds heavily on E2Former (Li et al., 2025), which already established the node-centric factorization — the incremental novelty is the hardware realization and the sparsification operator, which is narrower than the framing suggests.

Physical validation is thin: a single 216-water RDF and one 2 ns protein trajectory with no error bars, no convergence analysis, and comparison only to MACE-OFF. This supports 'stable' but not the stronger 'physically faithful' claim in the contributions.

Presentation has rough edges: broken references ('cuEquivarianceNVIDIA (2024)'), duplicated eSEN citations (2025a/2025b), minor inconsistencies between the main-text tensor-product setting and Appendix J, and the relationship between main-text Eq. (7) and Appendix Eq. (35) is confusingly presented across the two formulations.

Contribution 3 claims improved 'training throughput', but the evidence for training-time benefits (as opposed to inference/memory) is only the Table 4 ablation whose setting (train vs. eval) is not clearly stated.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies and motivates a real bottleneck in equivariant GNNs: edge-centric materialization of geometric features in HBM, and provides a coherent two-part solution (algebraic SO(3)→SO(2) sparsification plus a fused, node-centric streaming kernel).

The theoretical core is well developed: Lemma 4.1 (pole sparsity of solid harmonics in the aligned frame), Definition 4.2, and Proposition 4.3 are derived with full proofs in Appendix C, including the real-vs-complex CG basis change and parity selection rules, and concrete low-degree examples that make the re-indexing operator verifiable.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: accuracy on SPICE, OMol25, and OC20; kernel microbenchmarks against cuEquivariance and OpenEquivariance (Table 3); end-to-end component ablation (Table 4); throughput and memory scaling to 100k atoms against many baselines (Table 5); neighbor-density sensitivity analysis (Appendix E); and physical validation via water RDF and 2 ns solvated-protein MD.

Reproducibility is strong: code release is stated, and Appendices A, H, I give exact timing protocols, system generation, OOM handling, and full training/backbone hyperparameters, including the exact tensor-product implementation flag.

The paper is honest about key trade-offs: Appendix D explicitly discusses where the non-linearity lives relative to EquiformerV2/eSEN, Appendix J shows dense FlashAttention achieves far higher absolute TFLOPS, and Appendix E admits edge-centric baselines can win for very small k. This transparent limitations treatment is commendable.
weaknesses: Accuracy claims are somewhat overstated relative to the tables: e.g., Table 1 shows eSEN-Cons achieves better overall energy MAE (0.23 vs 0.31) and Table 2 shows eSEN-Cons slightly better total error (8.25 vs 8.38), so the claim of 'lowest Energy and Force MAE across most subsets' and 'preserves predictive accuracy' needs more careful hedging; the contribution is best framed as accuracy-competitive at much higher throughput.

The headline '20× higher TFLOPS' is measured against a naive PyTorch implementation, a weak baseline; Appendix J concedes the kernel reaches only ~2 TFLOPS vs ~38 for dense SDPA at D=64, so the framing in the abstract/introduction inflates the practical magnitude of the kernel-level gain.

Figure 1 shows the advantage over a masked FlashAttention baseline is modest and the curves nearly converge at large N; the main win is memory scaling (O(N) vs O(Nk) activation memory), which should be foregrounded more than latency.

The fused kernel is benchmarked only in the forward pass; training-time benefits (backward through the fused kernel, autograd for conservative forces) are implied by end-to-end throughput but never isolated, and the neighbor budget (max_neighbors=32 in Table 10) differs from the ~50 neighbors used in the throughput benchmark setup.

Novelty is incremental over E2Former (Li et al., 2025), which already established the node-centric factorization; the contribution is the SO(2) sparsification and hardware realization. This is valuable but the positioning as a new architecture ('V2') somewhat overstates the algorithmic delta.

Minor presentation issues: Table 8 (OC20) shows E2Former-V2 matching but not exceeding EquiformerV2 accuracy, and the TM-score analysis in Fig. 4b/Appendix K is qualitative without error bars or baseline comparison.
